questions.q: Why is an alert's raw severity label described as "a starting point, not a verdict"?
options: Severity is calculated from the alert type in isolation and has no idea whether the affected resource is a disposable sandbox or a production, privilege-bearing system
Severity labels are randomly assigned and carry no useful information at all
Only Low-severity alerts are ever worth investigating
Severity is set manually by an analyst before the alert is even generated
questions.explain: Severity is calculated from the alert type itself, independent of the specific resource's real-world context, which is why a Medium-severity finding on a critical resource can matter more than a High-severity one on an isolated sandbox.

questions.q: What does "blast radius" mean in the context of triaging a cloud security alert?
options: The physical distance between an attacker's location and the affected data center
The number of alerts generated per hour across the environment
How many security analysts are assigned to the triage queue
What identity privileges, network paths, and data a compromised resource could actually reach if the alert turns out to be real
questions.explain: Blast radius is about reachability from the affected resource — its attached identity's permissions, its network exposure, and the data it can touch — which is why the same alert can mean very different things on two different resources.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the correct way to handle a confirmed false-positive pattern, such as internal vulnerability scanning triggering brute-force alerts?
options: Permanently suppress that entire finding type across the whole environment with no further review
Document the specific, verified reason, scope any suppression as narrowly as the explanation allows, and revisit it periodically
Ignore all future alerts of any kind from the resource that triggered the false positive
Delete the alert from the console so it never appears in reporting
questions.explain: The lesson warns that blanket-suppressing an entire finding type is how a real attack resembling a known-benign pattern can slip through unnoticed — suppression should be narrowly scoped, documented, and periodically revisited.

questions.q: In the repeatable triage sequence described in this lesson, what should happen before an alert is fully closed out?
options: The alert should be closed immediately based solely on its severity label
The analyst should wait for a second identical alert before taking any action
Its claim should be correlated against a source-of-truth log like CloudTrail or Azure Activity Log, rather than trusting the alerting tool's summary alone
The resource involved should be deleted immediately in every case
questions.explain: The sequence closes with correlating the alert against the source-of-truth logs (CloudTrail or Azure Activity Log) before closing anything out, so the analyst isn't relying solely on the alerting tool's own summary.

questions.q: If a Defender for Cloud alert is already grouped into an incident, or Security Hub shows related findings on the same resource, what does this lesson recommend?
options: Treat each alert in the group as completely unrelated to the others
Automatically assume the grouping is a tool error and disregard it
Only investigate the first alert in the group and ignore the rest
Triage the group or related findings together as one connected story, rather than triaging the isolated alert tile alone
questions.explain: Checking for grouping is a dedicated step in the triage sequence precisely because related alerts tied into one incident or finding group tell a more complete, more actionable story than any single alert in isolation.
